article.title: What Alcohol Should You Give Your Boss?
article.body:
What Alcohol Should You Give Your Boss?

The safest alcohol gift for a boss is a recognisable bottle of champagne or a well-regarded single malt whisky, presented in a gift box with a short handwritten note. Drinks House 247 recommends staying modest on price, avoiding anything novelty or very strong, and confirming first that your boss drinks alcohol at all.

Buying a gift for the person you report to is harder than buying for a friend. Spend too little and it can look like an afterthought; spend too much and it can look like you are trying to win favour. Alcohol is a popular choice because a good bottle feels generous without being personal, but it only works if you choose carefully.

First, check that alcohol is appropriate

Before anything else, be confident your boss drinks. Many people do not, for religious, health or personal reasons, and they may not have mentioned it at work. If you have seen them order a drink at a work event, you are on safe ground. If you are unsure, a premium alcohol-free sparkling wine, a hamper, or something to eat is a better choice than a bottle they cannot use.

Also check your company's gift policy. Many organisations, particularly in finance, law and the public sector, set limits on gifts between colleagues or require them to be declared.

What are the safest choices?

Gift Why it works Best for
Non-vintage champagne from a well-known houseRecognisable, celebratory and easy to share at homeAlmost anyone, especially at the holidays or after a team success
A respected single malt whisky, around 12 years oldFeels considered without being showyA boss who drinks whisky or spirits
A good bottle of red wine from a classic regionWorks with dinner, low riskA boss who enjoys food and wine
A premium gin or tequila with its own gift boxModern and fun without being frivolousA younger team or a more relaxed workplace
A champagne and chocolate or flute gift setLooks complete and presents wellLeaving gifts and milestone celebrations

How much should you spend?

There is no fixed figure, but the principle is simple: a gift from a junior colleague to a senior one should be modest. A thoughtful mid-priced bottle is better than an expensive one. If you want to give something more substantial, make it a group gift from the team, which removes any awkwardness about one person trying to stand out.

When a manager gives gifts to their team, the etiquette reverses: it is normal for the more senior person to spend a little more, and to give the same or equivalent gift to everyone.

What should you avoid?

  • Novelty bottles and joke labels. They rarely land well with someone you work for.
  • Anything that hints at drinking a lot. Large-format bottles, shot glasses or "hangover kits" send the wrong message at work.
  • Very strong or obscure spirits. A cask-strength, heavily peated whisky is a great gift for an enthusiast, but a gamble for most people.
  • Something clearly too expensive. It can make the recipient uncomfortable and may breach a gift policy.
  • Giving it in public. Handing one person a bottle in front of the team can look like favouritism. Give it privately or as part of a team gift.

Reading the relationship

How well you know your boss should shape the gift. If you only know them professionally, stick to a recognised champagne. If you know their tastes, use that knowledge: a bottle from a whisky region they have mentioned, or a wine from a place they love to visit, shows you have listened, and that matters more than the price.

Presentation matters

A bottle in a carrier bag looks like a last-minute purchase. A gift box, ribbon and a short handwritten note make the same bottle feel deliberate. Keep the note brief and professional, for example thanking them for their support this year or congratulating them on a promotion.

When is it appropriate to give?

The most natural moments are the end-of-year holidays, a boss's leaving or retirement, a promotion, or a thank-you after a project they have supported. Birthdays are more personal, and in most offices a card from the team is enough. If the office has a Secret Santa, follow its spending limit rather than giving a separate gift.

Sending it to the office or home

Delivering to the office is convenient, and someone at reception can sign for it. For a leaving or retirement gift, sending it to their home with a note can feel more personal. Either way, whoever accepts it must be over 18, and the driver may ask for ID.

Frequently asked questions

Is it appropriate to give your boss alcohol?

Usually, if you know they drink and your company's gift policy allows it. Choose something modest and recognisable, such as champagne or a respected single malt, and give it privately.

How much should I spend on a gift for my boss?

Keep it modest. A thoughtful mid-priced bottle is better than an expensive one, and a larger budget works best as a group gift from the team.

What if I am not sure my boss drinks?

Choose something else, such as an alcohol-free sparkling wine, chocolates or a food hamper. Many people do not drink and may not have said so at work.

Is champagne a good gift for a boss?

Yes. A non-vintage champagne from a well-known house is one of the safest choices: it is recognisable, celebratory and easy to share.

Choosing the gift

Browse champagne gifts, alcohol gift sets and single malt whisky, or read about corporate alcohol gifts and how to send a gift anywhere in the UK. For more on choosing a top bottle, see our Dom Pérignon gift review.

article.summary: Recognisable champagne or a respected single malt is the safe bet. How to judge the relationship, what to avoid, budget etiquette and how to present it.
